utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present bar Pandurevic who sent his waiver. Prosecution today is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye. Defence teams absentees are Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. The witness is already here, so we can start. Between yesterday and today, were you approached by anyone or did you have any contact with anyone to discuss the subject matter of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no contact at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't discuss the case with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours, and good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Pajic. Yesterday when I left off, I was in the process of showing you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 2821.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that was in relation to your answer to a question that I put to you, which was: Whether or not you were shocked to hear that communications, along those lines, meaning the radio relay lines, had been intercepted. You indicated that you had not gained any information about that.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I wanted to show you was a communications plan that was prepared in connection with an Operation Stit which is signed by NATO Blagojevic, who is the chief of communications for the Drina Corps and Svetozar Andric, who was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could take you to point number 5 at this, which is at the bottom of the page I believe in your language, and on the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at point 2 under number 5 you can see that it reads: "Anti-electronic protection: The enemy are in a position to monitor and jam our command and control communications. In planning and using communications make certain that besides prescribed tactical and technical measures for protection, general and special documents for cryptographic protection are used." Now, did you receive any information concerning this particular issue at any time during your service in the war?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I am asking you in particular about what this document discusses, which is the ability of the enemy to monitor communications.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I pointed out yesterday, it was impossible to intercept secure communication lines. Those that were channeled through the encryption post. On protected lines of communication that were transmitted by a lower frequency, such as RR1 were possible to intercept. Specifically, I don't have any information indicating that any of the lines be channeled through the encryption post were, in fact, at any point intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, what about the lines that were not being channeled through the encryption or were not encrypted, did you have any information that those lines were being intercepted?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that type of information was never conveyed to me. If anyone, the security bodies might have been in possession of such information. They might have told the head of the signals unit. I, for one, was never told that. Had that not been the case, we would have requested for our frequencies to be altered or perhaps we would have sought alternative channels for our communication. To sum it up, I had no information indicating that any of our lines of communication were intercepted or tapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 3425.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In particular let me draw your attention to the first paragraph of the document, and it's a document that's dated 22nd April, 1993, and it indicates that it's signed by one Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. And in the first paragraph, second sentence it reads: "We have confirmation that the enemy is intensively intercepting our radio and radio relay communications, particularly active are their interception centres in Tuzla and in Trovrh (Gorazde)." Did you become aware of any information that's contained in this particular document? Not so much the document itself but the information that I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this document. I haven't seen it before. I did however know that the enemy did have interception centres at Trovrh and in the general Tuzla sector. Did I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had no information about the fact that they had the capacity to intercept VRS communications along radio and radio relay lines. That's your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I had no information. However, let me say this again. Radio relay lines that were transmitted over lower frequencies and those that were not protected or insecure could be intercepted, but I had no idea what technology they were using and what the frequency ranges were being used by them from the Trovrh and the Tuzla sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 3D00319.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like Mr. Vanderpuye to speak more directly into the microphone. It's difficult to hear. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I've heard that, and I'll comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document that is dated 23rd June, 1995, and it's type-signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic. In particular, this document reads, in the first paragraph anyway: "Through reconnaissance on the enemy's radio communication and information transmitted via radio, we have obtained information that our units are extremely careless when using communications equipment and do not verify the cryptographic data protection value of communications equipment ..." And it goes on: "Take all measures to ensure that these devices are not used to send documents classified confidential and higher, for they offer practically no protection of confidentiality." Now, it talks about different kinds of equipment that can be used to protect data and to send information that's less urgent because of the danger of that information falling into the wrong hands. Were you aware of information of this information? Not so much the document, but the information as concerns encrypted data protection?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't think of a specific example. Nevertheless, I must point out again that such telegrams, as were processed through the encrypted teleprinter station could not be intercepted or listened in. As for ROG12 and RRU1, those radio devices in particular, as long as they weren't secured, could be intercepted; and I believe I pointed this out on a number of occasions already. Even being unaware of this particular warning, I knew that this type of device, RUP12, RUP1, RUP33, RRU1 and other devices could be intercepted, but whenever a telegram was processed through a coded or encrypted teleprinter post, KZUS31, now that could not be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you don't disagree with what's actually in this document that you've just read, do you?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree as far as the open systems were concerned, meaning the devices that I've just enumerated, but whenever telegrams were coded, they could not be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic talks about verifying cryptographic data protection, he's not talking about open lines, is he? If you don't know what he's talking about, just let us know as well.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what lieutenant-colonel, which I think was his rank at the time, meant exactly. I completed a certain kind of training, then it wasn't possible for me to imagine that the enemy, given the equipment they were using, could possibly intercept our communication. I did not know, however, what the General based his assumption or suspicion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for that, Mr. Pajic. I think the document speaks for itself. But in terms of the actual process of encrypting or data protection along a radio relay route, how did that process actually occur? Was it automatic, did a person have to actually engage it? Tell us how that works.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if there was a hidden telegram that the -- had reached the teleprinter post -- are you asking me about protected written information or encrypted speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Encrypted speech, encrypted speech. That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Our device that I used to encrypt speech, cryptographic protection devices, KZU71, for example, if there was an open line, an open telephone line, it went into this device with a carrier waive, KZU71; it would get demodulated there and transformed into a code. Such a modulated signal would then go into 690 to 96 -- 610 to 960 megahertz, and then we had a carrier waive that we were using this device we could head a tone, but we couldn't hear the actual conversation. It was only the tone that carried. And then having reached the other end of the line, it would get demodulated and then there was a device with a certain frequency that would decode this speech and transform it back into an open signal. Such an encrypted conversation could be listened to by wire, KZU71 for example, and then when it reached the other end and came out of the KZU1, and then as along as it took to reach the actual phone. So that was the section in which you could actually hear the conversation. Everything aside from that was just an indistinct tone, not an actual communication conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And does that mean that the device had to be activated in order for -- does that mean that the device would have had to have been activated before the transmission occurs and some period of time allowed before the actual conversation is transmitted or does it mean that it could be operated instantaneously.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The device were operating on a permanent basis. It's not this was suddenly activated. They kept it operating throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as you're aware, in the radio route, let's call it from Vlasenica through Zvornik, that is Vlasenica to Veliki Zep, Veliki Zep to Cer, to Gucevo to Zvornik, and also down to Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka. Your understanding is that there was a protected route from Crna Rijeka to Vlasenica; that's the Drina Corps command, right? You mentioned yesterday about two routes, 0674 and 0607; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but before that let me tell you that the relay route between Vlasenica and Zvornik did not exist at all. There was none there between Veliki Zep and the command of the Drina Corps there were the two routes that I specified yesterday, and you have now brought up, one was the secure 0674 and there was one that was not protected in any way and that was the 0607 route.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you say there is no route between Vlasenica and Zvornik, you mean there is not a direct route, right? Because there is a way to communicate through the radio relay system between those two points, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about a direct route. There was no direct radio relay route between Vlasenica and Zvornik. There were other kinds of communication that we used and other relay routes through Veliki Zep, Cer, Rogatica, and Zvornik. Those were the points along the route that was used to convey, both spoken and written information between the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And those operators were with RR800 devices as you indicated, right, and FM200 devices?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were using RR800 between Cera and Gucevo, again RR800 between Gucevo and Zvornik, between Veliki Zep and Seren Kojista [phoen], SMC1306B; and as far as Vlasenica there were two routes, 0674 was M200 and 0607 was RR800.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to those routes, that is the route from Gucevo to Zvornik, that wasn't necessarily a protected route, was it?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the route from Veliki Zep to Cer, that was the SMC device that you talked about, there was also an RRU800 back-up device on that line; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, those were two routes, 1058 through the SMC that was operating; 0719 secure through the FM200 that was operating and the alternative route that was there; BB no number, RRU800 operating. This route was activated when the SMC was damaged during an air raid bombing in early September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to that bombing, by the way, were the frequencies changed after that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, when you mentioned that there was an annual plan with respect to these frequencies, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under the rules governing work at radio relay facilities, I'm telling you what was envisage, what the plan was, and not what was actually done. The annual plan provided for the annual frequency plan to be altered at some point; however, I told you yesterday why this didn't happen so the frequencies were not changed at any point between 1993 and 1995 -- or after 1995 for that matter. Therefore, given the fact that the frequency plan was changed within the army of Republika Srpska - and this was something that was ordered by the head of signals of the army of Republika Srpska - given the fact that Cer and Strazbenice were within the area of responsibility of the Yugoslav Army and the head of signals of the Yugoslav Army had to give this particular order, this would have implied a very complicated procedure; and we wanted to find a way around that and that was the simple reason why we never changed the frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You changed the radio paths, right? You changed the numbers for the paths, right? 0658, that's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was the one route where this was changed because of the documents there, because this route cropped up twice so we had to change it. The number, the number of the route was changed, but not the frequencies, not the devices that were used, or the distribution of channels, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of changing the number of the route if nothing else was changed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply we wanted to have the same numbers for the secure lines and the non-encrypted lines, non-protected lines, the chief of signals took that decision, but it wasn't about changing the frequencies or the distribution of channels. They were simply the number for this particular route that was changed. They were just about bringing our documents up to date on the secure lines and the numbers that we were using to talk to the corps, and then 00674 and 0658, those were two that were changed, and that was the extent of it. It wasn't about security-related reasons or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe there was a mistranslation in my question, but what was the purpose of changing the route number if nothing else changed? What did that accomplish, is my question.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one number was in Strazbenica and that was the same number used for a different feature. So we have the same number for two different features and that's why we changed that in order to avoid using the same number for two different routes and thus avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what number was that and how long were they the same? Maybe I will ask them separately. Let's start with what number was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that was the same for which routes?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Strazbenice, which was another feature, they had a route to a brigade in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long were these two numbers the same, that you're aware of, before they were changed?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're in charge of maintaining these lines, right? That's why you are able to tell us the route numbers, you're able to tell us the devices, you're able to tell us what was implemented when and why. You're now telling us that you had a situation where you had two numbers that were identical for completely different routes, and you don't know for what period of time that existed?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you that this was a route from a different relay feature. It wasn't within my area of responsibility. It was the army of Yugoslavia, the Strazbenice feature, it was their route. And then in order to not have the same number for one of their routes and one of ours, they asked that we change the number, and that was the reason. It wasn't my area of responsibility. I wasn't in charge of maintaining those devices therein that equipment, the equipment they were using. Strazbenice belonged to the army of Yugoslavia, that being the reason I can hardly say exactly when this happened or how long it had gone on for. The route was not at Veliki Zep. It was a different feature, and then we got a warning from them to the effect that we should change the number for our route because they were using the same number for one of theirs. We just wanted to avoid possible overlaps and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Already. So you have no idea how long this condition existed where you shared the same route number with -- you shared the same route number with Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No idea?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you get the warning to change it?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me. It was the chief of signals, and he had been cautioned by the chief of signals of the army of Yugoslavia and then my chief of signals said, The number for this route shall change tomorrow. As of tomorrow we are using this new one. It was the chief of signals who had conveyed that order to me. It wasn't me who took a decision on that particular change, nor did I get my information directly from the chief of signals from the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when did that occur? When were you told by your boss --

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in December. Sometime late that year 1995, probably December; but that's about as specific as I can be. It has been a long time, after all. It's been 13 or 14 years.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993. I'm sorry, December 1993. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This change that occurred, I just want to confirm for the record, was the result of an order from the Yugoslav Army to the VRS to change that route number; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I showed you yesterday a document that was 2823. And I don't think we need to put it in e-court, but as you testified to it yesterday, this was the October 2nd 1993 document. It was a Drina Corps document laying out a number of radio relay routes in corresponding frequencies and paths. You recall seeing that document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to a document of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I showed it to you yesterday. If you don't recall I can put it up on the screen so you can see it again.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, if you're referring to the one that mentioned frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am. Now, having read that document or having looked at it yesterday, did you see any indication on it as to protected frequencies or protected routes in relation to 0674, 0607 routes as you've described today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we see this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just trying to save time but it's no problem. It's 2823. If we could have that in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see which protected routes are mentioned. There is an error, MD310, so it is -- it should be MD310, AMD, because the device to protect speech was an AMD310 and two channels are used, 8 and 32. So the name of the device tells us that it is a protected route; whereas, a 12K could not be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what is the AMD320?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 310. Not 320. It's a mistake. There was no such device with the number 320 in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about 1993? Because that's when this document is dated.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That didn't exist?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It didn't exist. AMD310 existed, let me tell you once again. Its capacity was 32 channels, between 8 and 32 depending on the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would run on path 0674, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the path 0674, between Veliki Zep and the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. And from Veliki Zep to the command of the main -- of the VRS, I should say, the Main Staff? How does that signal get carried?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By an underground cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it has different radio -- it has a different radio path number, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every channel has two wires, and from the distributor at Veliki Zep it would be led to facility G1. So this was not a route number. A cable was used from Veliki Zep with eight pairs until the distributor in the room that we saw when we looked at the diagram of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down. You can see at point number 2, 0607?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that a protected line?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a protected line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go to point number 4. That one reads: "Command of the Zvornik Brigade Light Infantry Brigade ..." And then it says, "Towards Gucevo." Is that a protected line?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in view it has a carrier capacity. It is by a device that could not be protected, so the speech could not be protected because it was a carrier wave frequency and with this device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see on point number 4 it says frequencies of 880 and 810 megahertz. And you see that, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's written over something which we can't tell what's underneath it, but you can see those are the numbers that are assigned to it, and that falls within the range of an FM200 or an RRU800 device, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, only let me explain. All 8 channels or 12, or 34, that are working through this link, 1224, could not be protected as in the case of a protected route. When an entire route is protected, only one of the channels could be protected by means of the KZU. So KZU61 could protect only one of the channels selected from the 24 and not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you for that. Now, I wanted to ask you some questions also about the communications network, that is the radio or radio telephone network that you described in your direct examination. Now, first of all, are you aware of whether or whether or not any code names were changed as a result of documents falling into enemy hands in and around May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. This was done by an employee in crypto -- encryption department, Lieutenant-Colonel Radakovic, and when the codes got into the hands of the enemy then they had to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you recall whether or not that occurred in May of 1995 or not?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you with any certainty, I can't remember exactly, but I do know that the rule was if a conversation is intercepted by the enemy then the code had to be changed; but I can't remember exactly when that happened. I can't confirm it. It probably did but I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you 65 ter 3410, and let me see if that refreshes your recollection at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, this, as you can see is a document entitled --

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember these secret codes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is a document that's dated 5 May 1995, and you can see it's submitted to a number of different units. And it's signed by Radomir Prole, Colonel, and it indicates at the bottom of the page in the English and also, I believe, in your language: "Due to the new situation in the RSK and the suspicion that the documents of the communications plan in the Western Slavonia have fallen to the hands of the enemy. The existing code names of the units in command shall be changed according to the following ..." And it lists a number of different units. Does that refresh your recollection as concerns the questions I put to you before about the changing of code names?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this now. I frequently used these telephone secret codes, Panorama, Zenit; and you see the telegraph codes that were used when transmitting written information. And I remember when the names were changed, I forgot the exact time but I did use them when establishing radio relay links. So I am familiar with these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not the RS telephone net -- whether or not that was issued or changed in January of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, the radio telephone net of the Republika Srpska, what is that, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the radio devices that were used: RUP12, RUP1, RUP33, and the frequencies used by those devices. They have to be switched on if the net is active, so these are devices that are operating for reception, not for transmission. And transmission is switched on when a conversation is being transmitted. So these are the devices that I've already listed, RUP devices. They use low frequencies between 30 and 70 megahertz, and their radiation is circular. They need optical vision, their range is 10 kilometres when the range of vision is 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. I am a little puzzled by your answer, though. Is this document registration number 13 -- first of all, is it a document, and if it's a document, does it list different telephone extensions, frequencies, names, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an accompanying document, it must have also a review of the frequencies of the radio net.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you seen such a thing before?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would come across not orders but documents of this kind, reviews of code names, users of the radio network, I would come across them. This is just an attachment, an attached document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And as you are testifying here today, I went over with you just a moment ago the radio relay plan from the Drina Corps document that you looked at, do you have any idea what frequencies were actually operating in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which frequencies you have in mind, the number of frequency, the frequency range, or the actual radio relay device?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The frequencies that were operating on the routes that you described, 0607, 0674, and the other routes that you looked at in the document that I showed you from 1993. Do you have a present recollection of what frequencies were operating in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frequencies at the devices RRU800 and FM200, we are talking about these two relay routes, 0607 and 0674, the range was between 610 to 960. Now, the transmission and reception frequencies were determined. Say, the transmission frequency was, say, 783 on route 0674, in 1993, and the same applied in 1995. That is to say that the frequencies were not changed. This means that if the transmission frequency was, say, 783, then the reception frequency had to be -- the gap had to be 50 megahertz between the transmission and the reception frequency. And these frequencies did not change from 1993 to 1995. So it is within that range that the numbers of the emission and reception frequencies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you something. If you could just tell me, if you can recall, what is the frequency range, by the way, for an RRU800 device?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you I don't know how many times. 610 to 960 megahertz, 610 to 960 megahertz for RRU800, FM200, and RRU --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the maximum number of channels was 24 unprotected on the RRU800; on the FM200, between 8 and 32 protected channels. Told you this yesterday, and I repeat it today. I don't mind . MR. VANDERPUYE:

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. In terms of the routes -- well, let me just move on to a different question. utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a scheme, it connects the radio relay routes for the needs of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, the Eastern Bosnian Corps. These are analogue relay routes 0601. There was the Klekovaca, Kozara SMC device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't want to you to read the whole document. I just want to know what the title of it is. utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it on the diagram, and these connections that existed until the time that Jahorina was shelled, and then they disappeared after the communications hub on Jahorina was shelled; and as for 0661, as for this route, it went from Veliki Zep, Ravna, Romanija, Pale. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to know. It's not on this particular diagram, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on the diagram, I don't know who made this but this route to the government, 0661, did exist. It was a secure route.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as these two radio relay routes to Vlasenica are concerned, yes, it's correct. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is facing the opposite direction of the right-hand side -- no, no, now if we go up, that's it. All the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's it 0719, right? That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are certain things that are missing, that's true. It's not 1058, that's not the route number. It's not shown. Most of the channels that were used for the Drina Corps, or, rather, the Zvornik Brigade, and the Bratunac one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in addition to 0719 to Cer, there is route 1058, and an SMC device was used for this route.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And let me tell you the Drina Corps did not use radio relay routes 0719 for its needs. They only used the radio route 1058. So the Drina Corps did not use 0719, it used 1058 you exclusively.

utterances.text: Okay. So this document isn't accurate in that respect either, is it? It doesn't represent how things were laid out in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not accurate when it comes to 0719. That route did exist. However, secured links were used for the needs of the IBK, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and the army of Yugoslavia. utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you for that. Now, you maintain contact from the headquarters of the Main Staff with the Assembly, you said, with the presidency, you said; did you maintain contact from the Main Staff with the 10th Sabotage Unit in Vlasenica in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any direct connections to those units. So in the Main Staff we didn't have a direct link. We had to go through another exchange centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the same with respect to your connection, your ability to contact or maintain a connection with the 65th Protection Regiment in Novo Kasaba in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as the 65 protection regiment is concerned, which was located in Kasaba, there was on a radio relay device, RRU1 at Veliki Zep in Kasaba. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Naturally and travelling over an RRU1 line, the kind that you said could be intercepted, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only if a KZU71 had been set up, which served for protection, in such cases this device couldn't be intercepted; otherwise, if it wasn't protected by KZU71, then it would be possible to intercept communications on that device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And did you have a similar connection with a -- the command post in Borike in July 1995?

utterances.text: And you wanted no communicate from Borike, how would that go, how would that be accomplished?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that there was a radio relay device there, RRU1, at Borike, and there was a three-digit figure; I'm not sure which particular link you mean, but it was possible to get in touch with the Drina Corps. Primarily that's what we set it up for, for their needs, for the purposes of the Drina Corps and the Rogatica Brigade. The Drina Corps had a three-digit number as well, their own switchboard; therefore, they were able to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where was the actually building in Borike where this forward command post was located, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall specifically. For a while there was a holiday cottage right next to the hotel, later it was the hotel, the local office, this changed over time and I forget where it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you can't recall where it was in 1995, as it were, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if you wanted to send a document, not over an RRU1, perhaps an encrypted document, how would you do that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any need to send any document like that. It was probably done by the Drina Corps with the subordinate brigades. The communication lines went to the Drina Corps, and then the Drina Corps with its brigades would establish communication. I had no need at all to send any documents like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question is inartful again, and I apologise. I am not asking about what you did personally, I am asking about how would one go about sending a document if one were at the forward command post in Borike? How would you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could dial directly by using the three-digit automatic number, or you could use the switchboard in the Drina Corps. The Drina Corps was directly in touch with the Rogatica Brigade, the route being 0793 to Strazbenice and then 0695 to Rogatica, and that's how the communication happened. Between Rogatica and Borike there was a wire connection or a postal system that used to operate before the war so there was a cable already in place linking Rogatica to Borike. So it could have been a direct link through the Drina Corps central, hub Drina Corps through the central communications up to Rogatica and then by wire to Rogatica or directly through RRU1 and the three-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you send a document -- an encrypted document, from Borike directly? In other words, did they have encryption equipment in Borike as far as you know in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have that sort of equipment back 1995. I do remember that. Just in Rogatica at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if you wanted to send an encrypted document from Borike would it make sense for you to get that document to the headquarters in Rogatica in order for it to be sent?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I am not really sure, but as far as I know they did have an encryption device at Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you don't recall exactly where the communications equipment was in Borike, let me ask you: Do you know where the communications equipment was with respect to your connection from the Main Staff with Pale?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that, the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think I will rephrase it. When you had connection between the Main Staff in Pale, who was in charge of the equipment that was maintained in Pale, the communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in charge of the radio relay equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did that line go to?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the radio relay route, where it went to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went via Veliki Zep, Veliki Zep, Ravno Romanija, the hill above Pale, Kalovite Stijene. That's what the hill was called; and then all the way down to the centre for communications and reporting at Pale. And the encryption device was stationed there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there a connection, a direct connection as you say between the Main Staff and the president's office?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where did that line go, the one that connected to the president's office? Was it direct or was it indirect?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a direct line. There was also the automatic three-digit number that was installed in the president's office, and you could use direct dialing but you could go indirectly as well. There was a direct channel linking the president to the commander, and then there was the automatic three-digit number which could be dialed directly; therefore, it was accessible from the central switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you responsible for maintaining that equipment, that is, the equipment on the president's end of the communications network?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responsible for the operating of the radio relay equipment at Veliki Zep. At the other end, at Pale, there was the crew from the signal's battalion of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and they were in charge of maintaining communications there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as a practical matter, it didn't involve much for the president to actually have access to that line, just to pick up the phone from his office; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would have to pick up the receiver and he would have to actually dial the three-digit number, or press a button to make a call.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that a dedicated encrypted line or was that a line that might be protected or not be protected?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a special secure line. It worked along the protected radio relay route as all the other channels and the KZU71 device was used, same as all the other routes to all the other corps commands. KZU71, that was the device used to protect this route. Nothing special as compared to all the other protected routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So in other words it's not a device that's actually sitting in the office, it's a device that's located somewhere where the office connects -- the office line connects, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That, you said, is maintained by a unit from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The signals battalion of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And by the way do you know anybody from that particular signals battalion? Can you tell us people that you were in contact with, their names and such?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can: Captain Nenad Gracanin, Captain Nedeljko Planojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these would be two individual that would be responsible for maintaining the integrity of the encrypted line, the KZ device that you spoke about, as well as the regular line from the president's office outward?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these specific people were in charge of maintaining the radio relay route and keeping the line operating, the carrier way device between the distributor itself and the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were there any other communication -- I'm sorry, any other communication devices or routes that were used to allow the president to communicate with the Main Staff that you are aware of besides the radio relay routes as you've described?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could use PTT numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware if those particular lines went directly into the president's office as well?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about automatic telephone numbers, from existing telephone switchboards or hubs; for example, the one at Pale, they could have used direct dialing to get in touch. At the Main Staff there were PTT connections established by the post office. At Han Pijesak they could have used PTT connections directly and not rely on our military links, and they could still communicate. This wasn't really the case that often, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So these are regular civilian lines like you would use today, pretty much?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And those were available from the president's office. Can you tell us where the president's office was in July of 1995 if you know, what building it was in, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you had mentioned yesterday in relation to 65 ter 183, I believe it was, that the Main Staff didn't have an RU2/2K device. But earlier on in your testimony you were asked a question about the type of equipment that was used, and you said: "That the RU2K -- RU2/2K - I'm sorry - RUP12 and radio telephones were types of equipment most frequency used." And I just wanted to clarify that a little bit on the record because I'm not sure exactly what you meant by that. That's at page 28764 in the record. It wasn't the case that the Main Staff had an RU2/2K in 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a device like that. But I said yesterday this was hardly ever used, hardly ever, not that I was aware of, but there existed a device like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to clarify that because it wasn't clear to me and I appreciate your answer. You were also asked a question about extension 155 and whether or not that particular extension corresponded to more than one location in 1995. And I wasn't clear on your answer with respect to that either, because at one point you indicated that it corresponded to a forward command post, I believe you said that was in Jasenica, and then one in Jahorina; and then you said that it wasn't transferred in 1995. I am not sure what you meant by that. Was extension 155 in operation in the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka in 1995, in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the extension was in use in the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka in 1995. It was installed at four different physical locations in Crna Rijeka itself. But when I talked about 1995, about it being used, but what I said was that it had been used at Jahorina, at the forward command post back in 1993. In 1995 it was a different three-digit number. I can't remember which one exactly. 155 was operating in July 1995 at four different locations -- or, rather, it was installed in four different locations at Crna Rijeka, in the underground facility, and in two other rooms, and in the cabins there were two outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if you wanted to reach General Miletic, for example, in July 1995, it would make sense to call that extension, wouldn't it, 155?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the number was the personal number for General Milovanovic, chief of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. He had ordered for that number to be installed also at the operations centre, so it was. Given the fact that General Miletic was spending most of his time at the operations centre, he was always there, he was normally the person who responded to that number. If it wasn't him, it was probably the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let my just -- and by the way, do you know how long in 1995 extension 190 -- 155 was in operation or connected to Crna Rijeka as you've said?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was permanently connected and permanently operating. We never switched it off. One thing, it was installed at four different locations; and then the operations centre was in the underground facility, then we would use so-called debt-securing devices, to switch off the number to the cabins; but as of the 25th of May 1995 and onwards up until the end of September, the operations centre was, in fact, in the underground facility, then it was being used above-ground and it had two locations, the operations centre and room number 9, which is where the chief of the Main Staff was staying or where he was supposed to be staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 3935.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept as you can see, it's dated 6 October 1995. You can see in the title that it's from the state security service in Tuzla, and it purports to be captured on 642.00 -- well, 642.000 megahertz, 1210 on that day. And in that conversation -- just a second, let me make sure I have it correctly in front of you in your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the second page of the B/C/S, and it's on the bottom, it's 1531 -- yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see here -- you can read this intercept. It says that it was captured at 642.000 megahertz, and it's a conversation between somebody named Ljubo Jevic and an unidentified person in this conversation. About halfway down you can see where it reads: "I know, but why Arsic doesn't call extension 250 directly and cut it all short. I've sent it down there to General Miletic as well ..." It goes on and you can see he asks, later on, X asked: "Well, that was yesterday, I didn't want to go there until they send it because I'm in trouble, you know, I really don't know what to do anymore. Tell me, is he still on 155?" And then it says: "On 250, I'm going to call him right away." That's on the bottom of the intercept. Now, would it have made sense to try to reach General Miletic at extension 155 in October of 1995? And if you could also tell us what does extension 250 correspond to?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could use 155 to get in touch with General Miletic. As for 250, that is another three-digit number which was installed somewhere in the cabins. I am not sure in which room exactly, it had to be nearby, so probably it was just moved to an adjacent office. I can't remember specifically who the number belonged to, the 250 number. It's near 155. It must have been one of the adjacent offices or thereabouts. There were a number of these numbers being used and the automatic switchboard had a total of 250 such numbers. Each of the rooms had a three-digit number, so it must have been one of the rooms right there, nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Could I have 65 ter 3934 in e-court, please. Could we not broadcast this -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Will you take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an intercept, and it's dated 10 September 1995. It's also from the state security services at Tuzla, and it indicates that on frequency 641000 that they recorded a conversation involving, it says, between a general of the aggressor's army, Miletic, and some other participants from Panorama. And if you look immediately below that you can see it says: "M: General Miletic here, Panorama 155. In case there is some activities in the air, in the afternoon, inform Panorama 155 immediately because the agreement has been reached that the activity should stop for a while and we need information in case it is not being carried out." Now, with respect to this particular intercept, it seemed to indicate that General Miletic is speaking, and if it's connected to Panorama 155 that would indicate that he's at what location?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was at the command post of the Main Staff, but I don't know who he happened to be talking to at this time or where the other participant involved in this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it says here that it conveyed a message -- he conveyed a message to someone and to Zenit. Now, Zenit you saw on the document I showed you before ask that related to the Krajina Corps, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 3933 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another intercept. And this one is indicated to be from the 2nd Corps of the ABiH, and it indicates that it was delivered to their intelligence organ. It's dated 10 September 1995, like the other one; and the time of this one is 1710. Just so the record is clear, the time on the -- on 65 ter 3934 was 1746. In this particular intercept, it involves General Miletic and it says: "Operations duty officer, inaudible." It says: "GM: Give me operations duty officer. Hello, Pama here, tell me is there anything new at your place ..." And so on. I won't read the whole thing, but it says further on: "Something appears somewhere, call Panorama 155 immediately. Immediately inform Panorama 155." And it repeats that. Further on in the intercept we see that they note that General Miletic spoke on channel 7 and had a heated conversation with a duty officer, that the duty officer does not have Panorama 155 in his code book, so he doesn't know how to pass on the information. In this intercept, if you go to page 2 in the English, General Miletic tells him to look for Panorama in the ads, and once he finds it to ask for 155 and that's how he's going to pass the information where it's supposed to go in the end. Further on in the intercept, toward the bottom of the intercept in the English, and I think it might also be toward the bottom in the B/C/S, on the same page, it says that General Miletic asked another person, Zenit, a duty officer, he asked him as well to inform him of Panorama 155. That seems to indicate as well that General Miletic, as you say, is at Crna Rijeka as well, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these three intercepts all contain information that matches the reality of the situation in terms of the extension that is used and the person that is attached to that extension as it existed in September and October of 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am just not sure where the interception took place, at which segment of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you for that. I want to ask you about a different document. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 65 ter 3038, please. If I could have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. This is a -- well, it's an order, and at the bottom of it you will see that it is from General Mladic and it indicates -- well, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, it's 11 July 1995 and the strictly confidential number is 03/4-1616, and it's directed to the commands of the Drina Corps. In the translation -- the English translation. It reads the Zvornik Motorised Regiment. What it reads in the B/C/S is 65.zmtp. First, can you tell us what that is for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you tell us, Mr. Petrusic, I notice you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting my learned friend, but I'd like the whole document to be shown on the screen so that the witness can see it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or you can give him a copy of it if that is quicker and easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. President, I don't have a copy of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's show the whole document on the screen. How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's one page in the B/C/S and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, then it should be easy. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll direct him to specifically where I want him to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, in the header it indicates that it's directed to the command, and it says "65.zmtp." Do you see that? I just want you to tell us what that is, if you know, so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The header is not correct. If it's General Mladic's telegram, it should say the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, then his number. I find this very strange that in the header it only says "Republika Srpska." Also, I can't see what it says where the signature is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want you to tell me, if you can, what does 65.zmtp mean? I will get to the rest of the document in a minute, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This 65th Protected Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And among the units that it's directed to is also the 67th Communications Regiment and that's denoted as 67.PV, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 67th Communications Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And now if we could page down on this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, on this document you can see that it says "Komandant General Vukovnik [phoen], Ratko Mladic," and it's type-signed, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's indicated on the receipt stamp 1945 hours. You can see that, right? And also 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at point 4 of this document it says that: "The commands of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and the 67th Communications Regiment platoon," or regiment, I'm not sure how the translation reads, "are to ensure that the sound of air sirens. That at the sound of air raid sirens reasons all available personnel go to the shelters, the unit commanders are responsible to me for carrying out this order." Do you see that written there?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at point number 3, it indicates, in addition to its present tasks, the command of the 67th Communication Regiment is to provide one rapid reaction platoon for the deployment at the KM Main Staff VRS -- well, it says command post of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska and other -- and another in the Han Pijesak barracks for outside intervention toward the command post. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware of what is indicated in this order with regard to the deployment of 67th regiment members and both to the Main Staff and the Han Pijesak barracks, and also with respect to making sure that at the sound of air raid sirens, personnel go to their shelters. Were you aware of that on the 11th of July on the day that you had this party?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that this particular document raised some suspicions in your mind; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this telegram, which was received by the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, their encoder, it was not done properly. The telegram should have reached the Drina Corps. It should be reprocessed and then sent to the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. So it is an incorrect telegram. They simply forwarded this telegram without processing it at the encryption station at the command of the Drina Corps. So the telegram to the 2nd Romanija Brigade should have been signed and approved by the commander of the Drina Corps, because General Mladic or our encoder could not have sent such a telegram directly to the 2nd Romanija Brigade, and I don't remember this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't remember it? Okay. Well, you were a member of the 67th Communication Regiment, right? On the day that this order with you issued, 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member, and I do not remember that on that day there was any kind of an alarm in connection with any threat from the air. Everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it's clear here from this order that this was an order that was directed to your unit and concerned matters of relevance to your unit on the 11th of July 1995 and also involved personnel from your unit, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personnel was in the underground facility G1, so we couldn't take any special measures; and if this order was received, it was received by the commander of the 67th Communications Regiment, but I was not aware of it; so the company for garrison communications of the 67th regiment was constantly staying under ground, so there was no need for the commander to inform us about any special measures in the case of threat from the air or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, who would have formed this -- who would have formed this rapid reaction platoon for deployment in the 67th Communications Regiment? Who would that involve, what people?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 67th regiment had two battalions and a company for garrison communications. One battalion was at Crna Rijeka, where the cabins were, and it the other one was in the barracks in Han Pijesak, so the 67th regiment, in addition to the company for garrison communications that I was in, it had two battalions. One was at the command post, the so-called Barake [phoen]; and the other in Han Pijesak, so this probably applies to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you, the person charged with maintaining and setting up communications lines, have no recollection or had no involvement in this relative to this particular order, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You do know certainly now that VRS positions were in fact bombed on that day?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have no recollection of that as you have no recollection of this order, right?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, because the bombing was a daily occurrence, so I didn't devote special attention to it; and I really can't remember this order. It is addressed to the commander, and I was not at the encoding station, so I didn't control the receipt and transmission of such telegrams. It is true that it refers to the 67th regiment, but this telegram was not drafted properly. But I'm not challenging that General Mladic may have sent it, but it was not properly written. And this order for the 67th regiment need not have been encoded at all, because it was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I may I have just one question, please bear with me for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Pajic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Is there redirect, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pajic, talking about this ordering I would like us to look at this document again P3038. And let us go in order. The header says "Republika Srpska." Could this document have been sent from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been sent from the Drina Corps, yes, it could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll down the document, to the bottom, so we can see paragraph 3. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In item 3 there are certain combat orders as I would call them, in the course of your service, in the army Republika Srpska, did you have any combat assignments?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never had any combat assignments. I worked exclusively on the maintenance and establishment of radio relay and wire communications and that is why I was not familiar with this order and that is what I told the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the stamp, the time mentioned, 1945, could you tell us what it relates to?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this telegram could not have gone in this way, because it says Republika Srpska at the top. Now, if it was -- if it was sent by the Drina Corps, then the stamp of reception should be there, a round stamp, the time it was processed, then the telegram is revised, and then it is sent from the Drina Corps to the 2nd Romanija Brigade with a different header. So the command of the Drina Corps would be at the header and the same contents and signed by the command of the Drina Corps. So in this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I let him go for a while because I didn't see clearly what you could have in mind, but I do now. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise, can we have the witness not -- I don't know if he speaks English or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much English do you know? How much English do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could you remove your headphones, please. No -- remove them, put them ... give them to the usher. Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to alert Mr. Petrusic and the Court to a potential problem. This document from the handwriting on it, the -- the triangle, it's my memory that this document was provided to us by Mr. Petrusic in the Krstic case. And that's confirmed by Ms. Stewart. I am not sure, and I don't think we have been able to find it in some other collection; so I believe Mr. Petrusic is our foundation for it. And he may not be challenging the authenticity of it. From his questions, I can't tell, but the witness certainly is. And I don't think that Mr. Petrusic should be in a position where he is challenging a document that he actually gave to the Prosecution. This was always going to be a potential problem. We thought that it wouldn't be so much that Ms. Fauveau could take over in situations like this, but I just wanted to alert everyone to that problem. I haven't heard Mr. Petrusic challenge the document, but he's asking questions about it and the witness is, and given the situation where it came from, I just wanted to alert everyone to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you challenging the document, Mr. Petrusic? Let's make that clear first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps Madam Fauveau can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We are not challenging this document or its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Does that change the position for you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that helps, but as this witness goes down the road he's going, you've got the same problem, but we're -- I think we are okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are okay at this stage. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The problem becomes, Mr. President, if the witness challenges the authenticity, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then ask where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it seems there is one reason why I let the witness goes on and on is precisely so that we could have his answer already given that would solve your problem, unless he continues, of course; because if he continues that could create a problems too. But let's see. Can you please. Do you have anything else to add to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing. I just wanted to say that it was incorrectly sent. I am not denying that the 2nd Romanija Brigade received this telegram from the Drina Corps. Only thing is that it should have been drafted differently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because this was not our practice to work in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your next question, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question was, and I repeat it, could this document have -- could this document have left the Drina Corps with the signature of General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules in the teleprinter station, it could not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, when the officers were staying in the underground facility, could you tell us how many officers would be in the operations room, in room number 2?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I know that General Miletic who was there, that the operations duty officer would be there. I would see Captain -- was it Micic or Micevic I can't remember. Colonel Sokanovic, I would see him there occasionally, too. Three, four, or five. It depended. I cannot give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could each of them have answered and taken the receiver at 155?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could have. Usually it was General Miletic, but if he left the room or go to another one, then the officer on duty -- or one of the officers. Anyone could have answered the call if General Milovanovic was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Finally, your memories of October and -- September and October 1995, do you know where the officers from the Main Staff Command were staying?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September and October, once the bombing ceased, I can't remember the date, I think that was at the end of September, they would leave the underground facility and return to the so-called cabins, the compound. I don't know the exact date, whether it was the end of September, the beginning of November; in any event, it was once the bombing ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in September and the beginning of October, some officers from the Main Staff went to another theater of war?

utterances.speaker: VELO PAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the western Krajina battlefront, some officers did go there. In the zone of the responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic, we have come to the end of your testimony. We don't have any further questions for you, which means you are free to go. Our staff will assist you and arrange your return back home. Before you leave this courtroom, however, I want to make sure to wish you a safe journey back home and also thank you for having come over to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic -- Mr. Petrusic, you have five documents on the list. It has been circulated. Any objections from the other Defence teams? None. Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these five documents are admitted. I take it there are no documents from any of the other Defence teams, in any case it was only basically Mr. Krgovic putting some questions. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have also five documents which have been used in the course of your cross-examination. Any objections, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it there are no objections from the other Defence teams? Hearing none, the decision is to admit these documents as well. And we move to the next witness. Do you wish to make any statements before we start with the next witness, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just as a matter of caution it would be useful to inform the witness of his rights pursuant to Rule 90(e) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking about of Ratko Miljanovic, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Miljanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I extend a welcome to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very soon we will start with your testimony. Before you commence, however, you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that you will be telling us the truth. If you read that text that you are being shown now aloud, that will be your solemn undertaking with us and that would be equivalent to an oath in several jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.
